name: Felix Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a parcel van for a regional courier, the rural run out of the depot by the ring road. About 90 miles of farm lanes and villages, 80 or so drops, and the mileage bonus is why I earn more than the town drivers. The courier's app gives me the list and I take the photos it asks for, and that's as far as I go with phones. Two evenings a week I deliver for the pizza place on the high street, through their app.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing people. The farmer's wife at Low Barn has a mug of tea out for me on Thursdays. What wears me out is the depot changing things every few months, new scanners, new rules, new screens. I'm getting married next summer to Grace, and I'd like things to stay put for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that I never believed the fuss in the first place. At the depot I'd tell the younger lads I told them so. I don't go online much, so I'd leave that to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on, which is all I want. I've driven the same 90 miles of farm lanes for six years. A computer that saves somebody ten minutes on a spreadsheet doesn't change a single gate I open. My pay and the wedding plans stay where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the rural run and the two pizza evenings. Grace and I have about 14,000 between us and we want 20,000 for a house deposit by the end of next year, so I'd keep putting 700 a month away. The wedding's at Grace's family church in June, and that's paid for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon. Nothing to sort out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that bothers you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The depot is always fiddling, cutting routes or adding drops. That's the only thing. If they cut the mileage bonus I'd notice, but I'd still be better off than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using any of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a thing. Grace does the bills and the phone stuff, and if they had an AI thing she'd use it, not me. I'm happy with paper and a pen.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the fuss, and tell the younger drivers so.
I'd leave the **online talk** to others; I rarely post.
think: Office AI changes **nothing** about his rural route or its gates.
His **pay** and wedding plans stay exactly as they are.
do: Keep the **rural run** and the two pizza evenings each week.
Save **700 a month** towards a 20,000 house deposit with Grace.
Leave any **AI tools** to Grace, who handles the bills.
feel: He feels **calm**, like a Sunday afternoon with nothing to sort out.
S0.quote: I've driven the same 90 miles of farm lanes for six years. A computer that saves somebody ten minutes on a spreadsheet doesn't change a single gate I open.
fieldNote: He values **stability** above all, especially with his wedding coming.
His only worry is the depot cutting the **mileage bonus**, not technology.
He hands anything digital to his fiancée **Grace**, which shows how far he avoids it.

steps.text: Keep the rural parcel run and two pizza evenings
Save 700 a month towards a 20,000 house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people in offices have it coming, if I'm blunt, since they've been telling us how to do our jobs for years. At the depot I'd say the vans still need drivers. At church I'd say we'd pray for the families it hits, and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let the computers take the office jobs if they must. Nobody's built a machine yet that knows which farm dog to watch for on the Hollow Lane drop. But I know the depot. If the office goes over to software, the software will want more drops from me in the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much. I'd keep saving and maybe put the house a few months later, so we had a bit more in the bank. If the depot brings in a new AI routing thing, I'd use it because I'd have to, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd ask my uncle Samuel, who's a plumber, whether he still needs a hand on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. My job looks fine, but everyone around me would be changing, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to do anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, since I'm not asking for anything I haven't earned. If things got hard for people, I'd want the churches and families to step up first. Handouts just keep people at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Grace, does her work change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace works in the council's planning office, so she's the one with the screen job. If she lost hours, we'd still manage on my pay and the savings. But I'd want her to stay, she likes it.

At church I'd say we'll **pray** for the families it hits.
think: Software in the office would push **more drops** into his same hours.
Machines still can't know the **farm dogs** and quirks of his rural route.
do: Keep **saving** and push the house purchase back a few months.
Use any new **routing app** only because the depot requires it.
Ask his uncle Samuel about **Saturday plumbing** work.
feel: He feels **uneasy** because everything around him would be changing.
S1.quote: Let the computers take the office jobs if they must. Nobody's built a machine yet that knows which farm dog to watch for on the Hollow Lane drop.
fieldNote: He blames **office managers** rather than technology, showing an old grievance.
His fiancée's **council job** is the household's exposed income, and he notices it.
He prefers **church and family** support over government help.

steps.text: Push the house purchase back a few months to save more
Ask uncle Samuel about Saturday plumbing work
Carry on the rural parcel route as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have stopped it. At the depot I'd say the companies only care about the money. Online, for once, I'd probably write to the local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. My fiancée Grace and I planned a wedding, a house and three kids on this van. Robots by 2031 would take the van before the second child arrives. Grace's office job would go even sooner, in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house, straight away, and keep the deposit in the bank. I'd go to Uncle Samuel and ask to start a proper plumbing apprenticeship, even though I'd hate leaving the van. I'd keep driving full-time for as long as they'd have me. And I'd vote for whoever promised to slow the robots down, even if I didn't like the rest of what they said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep well. It's two jobs in one house, both gone inside five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Grace at the kitchen table and tell her we'd still get married, but the house waits. We'd stay in the flat above her parents' shop. Her dad offered it before, and I said no out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said no to that flat before. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride's cheap when you've got a house deposit. If it's both our jobs going, I'd take her dad's flat and be grateful. That's what families are for.

say: It's **madness**, and someone with power should have stopped it before now.
At the depot I'd say the companies only care about **money**.
For once I'd write to the **local MP**.
think: Robots by 2031 end his **driving job** before the children he plans.
Grace's **office job** would go even sooner, in 2028.
do: Freeze the **house purchase** and keep the deposit in the bank.
Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** with Uncle Samuel while still driving.
Vote for whoever promises to **slow the robots**.
feel: He feels **alarmed** and would not sleep well.
He sees **both incomes** in his home going within five years.
S2.quote: My fiancée Grace and I planned a wedding, a house and three kids on this van. Robots by 2031 would take the van before the second child arrives.
fieldNote: The threat to **both household incomes** turns his calm into alarm.
He would swallow his **pride** and accept his future father-in-law's flat.
Despite resisting change, he would start an **apprenticeship** at once.

steps.text: Freeze the house purchase and keep the deposit banked
Start a plumbing apprenticeship with Uncle Samuel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some years, so people should learn a proper trade. At church I'd say the young men should be apprenticed, like in our grandfathers' day. I'd still think the companies are rushing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still the end of driving for me. My father worked one job for thirty years. I'd be the first man in my family to be told his trade is finished at thirty-five. The few extra years only mean I see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house next year as planned, because Grace's job would last till 2031 and mine till 2034. I'd start Saturdays with Uncle Samuel in 2027 and go full-time with him around 2030. We'd keep a bigger cushion, maybe 10 months instead of 8. I wouldn't use the AI tools, but I'd let Grace use them for the household stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it's the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have the first baby, around 29 or 30. I'm not putting my family off for a machine. But maybe we'd stop at two instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How quickly do you think you'd pick up new things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow for me. I only use the phone for calls and the courier's app. If plumbing needs an app for invoices, I'd learn it, or Grace would.

The companies are still **rushing** it, even with a few years of warning.

feel: He feels **anxious**, less than in the fast picture but facing the same ending.
S3.quote: My father worked one job for thirty years. I'd be the first man in my family to be told his trade is finished at thirty-five.
fieldNote: His sense of **family history** makes the loss feel personal and shameful.

He admits he learns new tech **slowly** and leans on Grace.

steps.text: Buy the house next year while both jobs last
Work Saturdays with Uncle Samuel from 2027

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and folk who want work will find it. At the depot I'd say get a trade in your hands. I wouldn't be fussed online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends my driving, but I'd be 37, with the house sorted and the kids small. Ten years is enough time to learn plumbing from my uncle, and plumbing under a sink is the last thing a robot will ever do. That's what I'd tell myself, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house and get married as planned. I'd keep driving till around 2032 and help Uncle Samuel on Saturdays from 2029. Then I'd go over to plumbing for good. I'd keep the 8 months of savings and add to it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. It's far off, but I know where it ends, and I'd be starting again in my thirties with children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner than 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to know my job's safe till then. If the depot started letting drivers go early, around 2030, that would push me sooner. I'd go when Uncle Samuel can take me, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could robots do plumbing too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots that fix pipes? I don't know. Maybe one day. But I'd be in my forties by then, and somebody still has to show up at a house when it's flooding.

fieldNote: Even with ten years, the **certain end** of driving keeps him anxious.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because Grace's job and mine both go before we've had a chance. What would help is proper apprenticeships, paid, with real tradesmen, not courses on a screen. I don't want a cheque from the government. I want a job where somebody needs me to turn up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. That's where people would really go if it all fell apart. Not the government, the people you sit next to on a Sunday.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque from the government. I want a job where somebody needs me to turn up.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** rural parcel driver who earns a mileage bonus and does pizza evenings.
He is marrying **Grace** next summer and saving for a house; she works in the council's planning office.
He is **traditional and resistant**: he avoids AI tools and trusts church and family over government.
He stays calm in AI Plateau but becomes **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when both household jobs go.
Every AGI picture ends with him learning **plumbing** from his uncle Samuel.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when his job and **Grace's job** both go before they're ready.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** with real tradesmen, not courses on a screen.
Support from **church and family** rather than government cheques.
